name: Networking Fabric
blurb: InfiniBand, Ethernet, and interconnect topology for training clusters.

items.name: Arista AI networking
items.note: Ethernet switching platforms for AI back-end networks at hyperscalers

items.name: Quantum InfiniBand
items.note: The dominant training-cluster interconnect; the Mellanox acquisition that became NVIDIA's moat beyond the GPU

items.name: NVLink / NVSwitch
items.note: The intra-node and rack-scale GPU fabric; NVL72 puts 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain

items.name: Tomahawk switch silicon
items.note: Merchant Ethernet switch chips (51.2T Tomahawk 5 onward) powering AI clusters that choose Ethernet over InfiniBand

items.name: Ultra Ethernet Consortium
items.note: The industry effort to make Ethernet match InfiniBand for AI workloads; v1.0 specification 2025
items.maker: Linux Foundation members incl. AMD, Broadcom, Cisco, Meta, Microsoft

reading.body:
Networking within AI training clusters has bifurcated into an NVIDIA-dominated InfiniBand path and an Ethernet alternative backed by a consortium including AMD, Broadcom, Cisco, Meta, and Microsoft.

InfiniBand, acquired by NVIDIA through Mellanox, handles the highest-speed interconnection between training nodes at hyperscaler facilities. NVLink operates at a smaller scale, binding GPUs within single nodes and racks into unified compute domains. Arista and Broadcom provide Ethernet switching silicon and platforms as a competing architecture for cluster-wide interconnection.

This split matters because the physical wiring between thousands of GPUs during training creates a bottleneck separate from the compute itself. The choice between InfiniBand and Ethernet affects power consumption, latency, and the buildings required to house cooling infrastructure for the switches and cables. A cluster optimized for one standard cannot easily convert to another.

The emergence of the Ultra Ethernet Consortium and its 2025 specification indicates the market recognizes InfiniBand concentration as a constraint. The data shows competing approaches exist and are actively developed, but does not reveal which architecture actually dominates deployed AI training clusters by capacity or cost, or how the performance gap between them has evolved.
